content.text:
`range(start, end)` builds an array of consecutive integers. It starts at `start` and keeps pushing `i` while `i < end`, so the end value itself is never included: `range(1, 3)` returns `[1, 2]`.

That makes it a half-open range, the same convention as `Array.prototype.slice` and Python's `range`. Callers that want the end value included need `range(start, end + 1)`, and a call with `end <= start` returns an empty array because the loop condition is false on the first check.

`range(start, end)` builds an array of consecutive integers. It starts at `start` and keeps pushing `i` while `i < end`, so the end value itself is never included: `range(1, 3)` returns `[1, 2]`.

That makes it a half-open range, the same convention as `Array.prototype.slice` and Python's `range`. Callers that want the end value included need `range(start, end + 1)`, and a call with `end <= start` returns an empty array because the loop condition is false on the first check.

`range(start, end)` builds an array of consecutive integers. It starts at `start` and keeps pushing `i` while `i < end`, so the end value itself is never included: `range(1, 3)` returns `[1, 2]`.

That makes it a half-open range, the same convention as `Array.prototype.slice` and Python's `range`. Callers that want the end value included need `range(start, end + 1)`, and a call with `end <= start` returns an empty array because the loop condition is false on the first check.

That makes it a half-open range, the same convention as `Array.prototype.slice` and Python's `range`. Callers that want the end value included need `range(start, end + 1)`, and a call with `end <= start` returns an empty array because the loop condition is false on the first check.
